keyVerseText: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word אֵל (ʼêl) is etymologically derived as a shortened form of אַיִל (ʼayil), which fundamentally denotes strength and might, often symbolized by a ram or a strong tree such as an oak. This root emphasizes not only physical strength but also leadership and stability, which enriches the English gloss 'God' by highlighting the concept of divine power as a foundational and sustaining force rather than merely a title.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, אֵל (ʼêl) appears 246 times and is predominantly translated as 'God' in 73 instances, underscoring its primary use to denote deity or divine might. It also appears in idiomatic forms such as 'of God' and 'unto God,' reflecting relational aspects with the divine. While it can refer to any god or mighty one, including false gods or angels, the consistent range of translations reveals its broad semantic field centered on might, power, and deity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֵל as rooted in strength and might deepens our grasp of God's nature as supremely powerful and sovereign. This word conveys that God is not an abstract or distant force but the ultimate source of strength and stability, the Almighty who upholds all things. Recognizing that אֵל can refer to mighty men or angels also highlights God's supremacy above all created powers. For the Christian faith, this affirms the uniqueness of Jehovah as the one true God whose power is unmatched and who invites trust and worship.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 14:18 states, 'And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.' The use of אֵל here emphasizes the supreme might and sovereignty of the God whom Melchizedek served. It highlights that Melchizedek's priesthood is connected to the worship of the Almighty, reinforcing the understanding of God as the ultimate strong one who reigns above all earthly powers.
